tldr: To reduce manual labor and instability in physical robot testing, this paper proposes an evaluation pipeline that generates rollout videos in a calibrated simulator, evaluates pairwise behavior quality with VLMs, and ranks policies via the Bradley-Terry model.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of R2S-Eval. Rollout videos of multiple policies ($\pi_1 \sim \pi_6$) are gathered in a simulator calibrated to the real-world setting. A VLM then determines pairwise preferences on behavior quality, producing a final unified policy ranking.
overview:
With the rise of large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models, deploying robots to perform diverse tasks in physical environments is becoming a reality. However, policy evaluation remains a major bottleneck. Prevailing real-world evaluation relies heavily on manual work: human operators repeatedly reset objects, monitor robot executions, and log success or failure. This process is not only time-consuming, but also unstable, as slight shifts in initial object poses can flip the outcome. Most crucially, relying strictly on a binary 0-or-1 success rate fails to capture execution quality—whether a task succeeded smoothly and cleanly, or barely and clumsily.

To address this, the authors developed R2S-Eval, an evaluation framework that pairs simulation with vision-language models (VLMs). By matching camera poses and scene geometry to the physical setup in Isaac Sim, the pipeline generates abundant rollout videos. A VLM then inspects video pairs to judge which execution is better. Aggregating these pairwise judgments using a statistical preference model (the Bradley-Terry model) automatically produces reliable policy rankings that reflect nuanced human judgment.

In validation experiments across the standard LIBERO benchmark and a physical dual-arm, multi-fingered humanoid robot evaluating six modern VLA models, simulated success rates matched real-world results within a mean absolute error of just 2.13 percentage points, perfectly preserving policy rankings. Furthermore, VLM preference judgments achieved 82.9% agreement with human evaluators. The system reliably distinguished execution quality differences—such as motion smoothness and retry behavior—even between runs sharing the same success or failure outcome. This significantly curbs dangerous, exhausting hardware trials while enabling detailed, stable policy evaluation.
contributions: Reformulated robot policy evaluation from counting binary success rates into a ranking estimation problem based on rollout behavior preferences.

Proposed R2S-Eval, an evaluation pipeline that safely and efficiently collects rollout videos in a calibrated real-to-sim environment, evaluates them via VLMs, and aggregates preferences with the Bradley-Terry model.
Established a comprehensive five-axis validation protocol to assess evaluation pipeline soundness across reliability, stability, human agreement, operational effort, and behavioral informativeness.

sections.heading: Beyond Counting Successes: Why Physical Robot Evaluation Needs a Rethink
sections.summary: Real-world robot evaluation suffers from heavy manual effort and high variance, and coarse binary success rates fail to measure behavioral quality. Inspired by how humans intuitively compare videos, the authors combined simulation and VLMs to rank policies automatically and accurately.
sections.details:
Rapid progress in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has yielded generalist robot policies capable of handling diverse tasks. Yet, evaluating which policy is truly superior remains deeply challenging.

Typically, researchers fine-tune models per task, deploy them to hardware, and run repeated trials to tally success rates. This requires tedious manual labor, including resetting initial object configurations and constantly monitoring the robot. Moreover, minor variations in table friction or object placement cause results to fluctuate, leading to poor reproducibility across runs. A single success-rate metric also completely ignores execution quality: it cannot tell whether a task was completed with elegant precision or forced through clumsily.

When humans evaluate a robot, they look beyond binary outcomes. They consider trajectory smoothness and, in failure cases, how much progress was made toward the goal. This study proposes comparing rollout videos pairwise and estimating latent policy capability from these preferences. By collecting videos in simulation to spare hardware effort and using VLMs as evaluators in place of humans, the approach achieves both automation and quality-aware assessment.

sections.heading: Tracing the Roots: Automated Real-World Testing, Simulators, and LLM/VLM Judges
sections.summary: Robot evaluation has expanded toward simulated benchmarks and automated hardware setups, but remains dominated by success rates. Drawing inspiration from the success of LLM-as-a-Judge in conversational AI, this work extends pairwise preference evaluation to continuous robot behaviors.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main research foundations: robot evaluation benchmarks, real-to-sim environment reconstruction, and foundation-model evaluators.

### Robot Policy Benchmarks
Standardized benchmarks such as LIBERO and BEHAVIOR-1K offer reproducible simulated testing. While some physical systems introduce automated reset mechanisms, evaluation still primarily collapses into scalar task-completion or success rates, failing to capture differences in smoothness and stability.

### Real-to-Sim Reconstruction
Real-to-sim techniques using 3D Gaussian Splatting and physics engines increasingly recreate real environments in virtual spaces. Nevertheless, manipulation tasks with frequent contacts still suffer from physical gaps (the Sim-to-Real / Real-to-Sim gap) in friction and grasping.

### Evaluating Robot Behavior with VLMs
Recent works explore VLMs for detecting task success or verifying subgoals. In natural language processing, the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm has proven effective by having models compare two generated outputs pairwise. This research applies that concept to robot videos. Rather than assigning noisy absolute scores to individual rollouts, it statistically aggregates pairwise comparisons to construct robust, reliable policy rankings.

sections.heading: Under the Hood: From Real-to-Sim Rollouts to VLM Judges and Bradley-Terry Aggregation
sections.summary: The pipeline operates in three stages: generating rollouts in a simulator calibrated to real geometry and cameras, prompting a VLM to judge behavior quality between video pairs, and aggregating results using the Bradley-Terry model to yield capability scores and rankings.
sections.details:
Here is how R2S-Eval's algorithm and pipeline function step by step.

### III-A Problem Formulation
Traditional approaches rank policies by averaging rollout outcomes $c(\tau) \in \{0, 1\}$ into a success rate for policy $\pi_i$. In contrast, this study evaluates pairwise preference judgments $y_{ij}^{ab}$ between rollout videos $(v_i^a, v_j^b)$. By constructing a win-count matrix $M$ where policy $\pi_i$ outperforms $\pi_j$, the pipeline statistically estimates latent quality scores $\theta_i$.

### III-B Real-to-Sim Calibration
Because capturing extensive physical rollouts is demanding, the team builds a simulated environment $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{S}}$ calibrated to the physical environment $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{R}}$. Rather than chasing perfect visual photorealism, calibration focuses on action-critical factors: robot kinematics, joint limits, camera fields of view, and 3D object assets and poses.
A key innovation here is "adaptive policy training." Direct zero-shot transfer of real-world policies into simulation can produce unstable behaviors due to contact friction and compliance mismatches. Adapting policies on simulated rollout data yields robust simulation-ready policies $\pi_i^{\mathrm{S}}$. These policies execute closed-loop rollouts to collect video sets $\mathcal{V}_i$ efficiently.

### III-C VLM Preference Evaluation
Video pairs sharing the same task and initial conditions are sampled from the pool. Instead of asking for a raw preference, the VLM is first prompted to output structured textual descriptions detailing motion smoothness, temporal consistency, task progress, and contact control. It then compares the two rollouts against these criteria to deliver a binary preference. This two-stage prompt structure makes the rationale transparent.
From the preference matrix $M$, the Bradley-Terry (BT) model estimates latent scores $\theta_i$ via maximum likelihood estimation. Because the BT model formalizes the win probability of $\pi_i$ over $\pi_j$ as $q_{ij} = \frac{\exp(\theta_i)}{\exp(\theta_i) + \exp(\theta_j)}$, it derives an objective, unified skill metric across extensive match-ups.

### III-D Five-Axis Validation Protocol
To verify evaluation pipeline validity, the authors define five criteria: (1) reliability (agreement with real-world ground truth), (2) stability (robustness across repeated trials), (3) human agreement (alignment with human preferences), (4) operational effort (reduction in operator supervision time), and (5) behavioral informativeness (capturing differences beyond binary success).

sections.heading: Empirical Results: Putting R2S-Eval to the Test with a Dual-Arm Robot and Six VLAs
sections.summary: Evaluating six VLA policies on a 63-DoF dual-arm humanoid robot and in simulation revealed that R2S-Eval almost perfectly reproduced real-world rankings. VLM preferences matched human judgments at 82.9% and successfully discerned quality variations among rollouts with identical success outcomes.
sections.details:
To validate the framework, the authors conducted extensive experiments across physical hardware and simulation.

### Experimental Setup and Robot Platform
The physical testbed featured SharpaNorth, a 63-DoF dual-arm humanoid robot equipped with two 22-DoF dexterous hands. Tasks covered seven tabletop scenarios shown in Figure F3. The evaluation compared six prominent VLA models: $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, OpenVLA, NORA-Long, SmolVLA, and X-VLA. In Isaac Sim, simulation rollouts were generated automatically by replaying real teleoperation trajectories and looping through small initial-pose perturbation retries.

### IV-A Real-to-Sim Consistency (Q1)
In closed-loop rollouts across hardware and simulation, the average absolute difference in task success rates was only 2.13 percentage points (at most 7.0 points). Crucially, the overall policy ranking across all six models matched between reality and simulation. Beyond grouping top performers ($\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, X-VLA) apart from the rest, characteristic failure modes—such as micro-vibrations without progress or wide oscillations—were replicated consistently.

### IV-B Accuracy and Stability of VLM Judgments (Q2, Q3, Q4)
Across both the LIBERO benchmark and the real-to-sim environment, eight VLMs—including Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-OV-1.5, and Gemma 3—served as evaluators. On LIBERO, VLM preferences correlated strongly with real success rates (Spearman's $\rho = 0.823$, Pearson's $r = 0.924$). Agreement with human raters reached 82.9%. Swapping video order maintained 91.5% preference consistency, demonstrating resilience against position bias.

### IV-C Reducing Hardware Labor (Q3)
On physical hardware, operator effort for resets and supervision scales linearly with tasks and trials, creating massive bottlenecks. In contrast, once R2S-Eval calibrates the simulator, additional real-world testing time drops to zero while simulation rollouts scale automatically.

### IV-D Behavioral Informativeness Case Study (Q5)
The authors examined pairs with identical binary outcomes. As shown in Figure F8 (a), between two successful trials, the VLM preferred a smooth, single-attempt grasp over one requiring multiple clumsy retries. Similarly, in Figure F8 (b) between two failures, the VLM favored an arm reaching into the box toward the target over an arm vibrating aimlessly in place. This discriminative capability is impossible with binary metrics alone.

sections.heading: Looking Forward: Toward Scalable, Quality-Aware Robot Evaluation
sections.summary: R2S-Eval reduces the manual effort and variance of physical robot testing, using VLM vision to deliver reliable policy rankings that reflect execution quality. Future work will expand to mobile manipulation and refine contact physics modeling.
sections.details:
This paper introduced R2S-Eval, a novel evaluation framework for robot manipulation policies.

By marrying real-to-sim calibration with VLM-based pairwise preference evaluation, the framework addresses the three primary pain points of physical testing: high labor demands, unstable outcomes, and narrow success-rate metrics. Extensive experiments in simulation and on a physical humanoid robot confirm that it assesses policy capabilities closely aligned with human judgment.

Looking ahead, the authors plan to expand from tabletop setups to mobile manipulation involving whole-body coordination, as well as broader robotic form factors. They also aim to narrow the real-to-sim gap further through higher-fidelity contact physics modeling. As robot policy development accelerates, scalable, quality-aware evaluation frameworks like R2S-Eval will play an increasingly vital role.

takeaways: Shifting from binary success tallies (0/1) to pairwise video preferences aggregated via the Bradley-Terry model yields fair policy rankings that account for smoothness and recovery behavior.
Collecting closed-loop rollout videos with adaptive policy training in a real-to-sim environment eliminates the need for exhausting, hazardous physical testing loops.
Modern open-weight VLMs (such as Qwen and LLaVA) achieve over 80% agreement with human evaluators when guided by structured evaluation prompts.
limitations: Because real-to-sim gaps in contact and friction cannot be completely eliminated, policies require an extra adaptive training step before running reliably in simulation.
When comparing policies with nearly identical capabilities, VLMs exhibit a slight position bias toward the first video, though order shuffling helps mitigate this.
Experiments were restricted to static tabletop manipulation; whether this stability holds for long-horizon mobile manipulation remains unverified.
